'''Chronic wasting disease''' ('''CWD'''), sometimes called '''zombie deer disease''', is a [[transmissible spongiform encephalopathy]] (TSE) naturally affecting [[Deer|members of the deer family]]. TSEs are a family of diseases caused by misfolded proteins called [[prions]] and include similar diseases such as [[Bovine spongiform encephalopathy|mad cow disease]] in cattle, [[Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease]] in humans, and [[scrapie]] in sheep.<ref name=cwdfacts>{{cite web |url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/nvap/reference-guide/control-eradication/cwd |title=Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) |publisher=USDA |agency=APHIS |date=2020-06-02 |access-date=2023-12-27}}</ref> In the [[United States]], CWD affects [[mule deer]], [[white-tailed deer]], [[red deer]], [[sika deer]], [[elk]], [[caribou]], and [[moose]].<ref name=USDA/> The transmission of CWD to other species such as [[squirrel monkey]]s and [[Humanized mouse|humanized mice]] has been observed in experimental settings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/prions/cwd/transmission.html|title=Transmission {{!}} Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) {{!}} Prion Disease {{!}} CDC|date=2018-12-03|website=www.cdc.gov|access-date=2019-02-21}}</ref>

In 1967, CWD was first identified in mule deer at a government research facility in northern [[Colorado]], United States.<ref name=USDA/> It was initially recognized as a clinical [[Cachexia|"wasting" syndrome]] and then in 1978, it was identified more specifically as a TSE disease. Since then, CWD has been found in free-ranging and captive animal populations in 33 US states and five Canadian provinces.<ref name="NWHC">
{{cite web |date=2022-04-01 |title=Distribution of Chronic Wasting Disease in North America |url=https://www.usgs.gov/media/images/distribution-chronic-wasting-disease-north-america-0 |access-date=2022-08-29 |website=USGS.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Chronic wasting disease {{!}} ontario.ca |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/chronic-wasting-disease |access-date=2025-02-13 |website=www.ontario.ca |date=17 July 2014 |language=en}}</ref> In addition, CWD has been found in one Minnesota [[red deer]] farm, one wild reindeer herd in [[Norway]] (March 2016) as well as in wild moose. Single cases of CWD in moose have been found in [[Finland]] (March 2018) and in [[Sweden]] (March and May 2019, September 2020). CWD was found in [[South Korea]] in some deer imported from [[Canada]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/prions/cwd/occurrence.html|title=Occurrence {{!}} Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) {{!}} Prion Disease {{!}} CDC|date=2019-02-25|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us|access-date=2019-03-05}}</ref> CWD is typified by chronic weight loss and clinical signs compatible with brain lesions, aggravated over time, always leading to death. 

Although reports in the popular press have been made of humans being affected by CWD, a 2004 study for the US [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] concluded that "more epidemiologic and == Signs and symptoms ==
Due to CWD taking 18–24 months after initial exposure to onset, most cases of CWD occur in adult animals; the youngest animal to exhibit clinical symptoms of the disease was 15 months.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.inspection.gc.ca/animals/terrestrial-animals/diseases/reportable/cwd/if-your-animals-may-be-infected/eng/1330188848236/1330189018195| title=Chronic wasting disease - What to expect if your animals may be infected| website=Canadian Food Inspection Agency|access-date=10 April 2019|date=1 April 2019}}</ref> The disease is progressive and always fatal. The first signs are difficulties in movement.  The most obvious and consistent clinical sign of CWD is weight loss over time. Behavioral changes also occur in the majority of cases, including decreased interactions with other animals, listlessness, lowering of the head, tremors, repetitive walking in set patterns, and nervousness. Excessive salivation and grinding of the teeth also are observed. Most deer show increased drinking and urination; the increased drinking and salivation may contribute to the spread of the disease.<ref name=2015rev>{{cite journal |pmid=25387112 |year=2015 |last1=Haley |first1=N. J. |title=Chronic wasting disease of cervids: Current knowledge and future perspectives |journal=Annual Review of Animal Biosciences |volume=3 |pages=305–25 |last2=Hoover |first2=E. A. |doi=10.1146/annurev-animal-022114-111001 }}</ref> Loss of fear of humans and appearance of confusion are also common.<ref name="WCTCWDA">{{cite web |title=Minnesota landfill to burn deer carcasses in effort to prevent CWD spread |url=https://wctrib.com/incoming/4711337-Minnesota-landfill-to-burn-deer-carcasses-in-effort-to-prevent-CWD-spread |publisher=wctrib.com |date=8 October 2019 |access-date=22 October 2019 |archive-date=9 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109221406/https://www.wctrib.com/incoming/4711337-Minnesota-landfill-to-burn-deer-carcasses-in-effort-to-prevent-CWD-spread |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service]] summarized it as:<ref name=USDA/>
{{cquote|Behavioral changes, emaciation, weakness, [[ataxia]], salivation, aspiration pneumonia, progressive death.}}

== Cause ==
The cause of CWD (like other TSEs, such as [[scrapie]] and [[bovine spongiform encephalopathy]]) is a [[prion]], a misfolded form of a normal [[protein]], known as prion protein (PrP), that is most commonly found in the [[central nervous system]] and [[peripheral nervous system]]. The misfolded form has been shown to be capable of converting normally folded prion protein, PrP<sup>C</sup> ("C" for cellular) into an abnormal form, PrP<sup>Sc</sup> ("Sc" for scrapie), thus leading to a chain reaction. CWD is thought to be transmitted by this mechanism. The abnormality in PrP has its genetic basis in a particular variant of the protein-coding gene ''[[PRNP]]'' that is highly conserved among mammals and has been found and sequenced in deer. The build-up of PrP<sup>d</sup> in the brain is associated with widespread [[neurodegenerative disease|neurodegeneration]].<ref name=USDA>{{cite conference |author=Patrice N Klein, CWD Program Manager USDA/APHIS |url=http://www.fws.gov/whhcc/doc/CWD%20Overview.pdf |title=Chronic Wasting Disease - Review of Disease Transmission and Control |conference=WHHCC Meeting |date=5–6 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140926165354/https://www.fws.gov/whhcc/doc/CWD%20Overview.pdf |archive-date=26 September 2014}}</ref><ref name=2015rev/><ref name=NWHCFAQ>{{cite web |title=USGS National Wildlife Health Center - Chronic Wasting Disease FAQ |url=https://www.nwhc.usgs.gov/disease_information/chronic_wasting_disease/frequently_asked_questions.jsp |access-date=April 25, 2016 |date=19 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160319012545/http://www.nwhc.usgs.gov/disease_information/chronic_wasting_disease/frequently_asked_questions.jsp |archive-date=19 March 2016 }}</ref>

===Genetics===
The [[allele]] which encodes [[leucine]], [[codon]] 132 in the family of Elks, is either [[homozygous]] LL, homozygous MM, or [[heterozygous]] ML. Individuals with the first encoding seem to resist clinical signs of CWD, whereas individuals with either of the other two encodings have much shorter incubation periods.<ref name=USDA/>

In white-tailed deer, [[Gene polymorphism|polymorphisms]] at codons 95 (Q->H) and 96 (G->S) dramatically affect CWD progression and prion strain specification. Deer containing the 96S allele have delayed progression to clinical disease onset.<ref name=ualb>{{cite journal |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0017450|pmid=21445256|pmc=3060816|title=Prion Protein Polymorphisms Affect Chronic Wasting Disease Progression|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=6|issue=3|article-number=e17450|year=2011|last1=Johnson|first1=Chad J.|last2=Herbst|first2=Allen|last3=Duque-Velasquez|first3=Camilo|last4=Vanderloo|first4=Joshua P.|last5=Bochsler|first5=Phil|last6=Chappell|first6=Rick|last7=McKenzie|first7=Debbie|bibcode=2011PLoSO...617450J|doi-access=free}}</ref>

When deer with the 95H polymorphism become infected, they select for altered strains of CWD.<ref name=EID>{{cite journal |doi=10.3201/eid2309.161474|pmid=28820384|pmc=5572867|title=Chronic Wasting Disease Prion Strain Emergence and Host Range Expansion|journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases|volume=23|issue=9|pages=1598–1600|year=2017|last1=Herbst|first1=Allen |last2=Velásquez |first2=Camilo|last3=Triscott|first3=Elizabeth|last4=Aikeno|first4=Judd|last5=McKenzie|first5=Debbie}}</ref>

=== Spread ===
Researchers in July 2019 stated that "with all the research on the malignity of prions, and the permanence of prions in the wider environment, and their resistance to destruction and degradation, it is necessary to reduce the potential sources of exposure to CWD."<ref name="acia">{{cite news |title=Maladie débilitante chronique: le public exposé à des risques |first=Morgan|last=Lowrie |url=https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/sante/201907/31/01-5235800-maladie-debilitante-chronique-le-public-expose-a-des-risques.php |publisher=La Presse Canadienne |date=31 July 2019 |access-date=29 December 2023}}</ref> In fact an [[APHIS]] scientist observed that, while the longevity of CWD prion is unknown, the [[scrapie]] prion has been measured to endure for 16 years.<ref name=USDA/><ref name=p2001/> PrP<sup>CWD</sup> is insoluble in all but the strongest solvents, and highly resistant to [[digestion]] by [[proteases]].<ref name=USDA/> PrP<sup>CWD</sup> converts the normal protein PrP<sup>C</sup> into more of itself upon contact, and binds together forming aggregates.<ref name=USDA/><ref name=p2001>{{cite journal |pmid=11357156|doi=10.1056/NEJM200105173442006|title=Neurodegenerative Diseases and Prions|journal=New England Journal of Medicine|volume=344|issue=20|pages=1516–1526|year=2001|last1=Prusiner|first1=Stanley B.|doi-access=free}}</ref> Prusiner noted in 2001 that:<ref name=p2001/>

{{cquote|In the prion diseases, the initial formation of PrP<sup>Sc</sup> leads to an [[Exponential growth|exponential increase]] in the protein, which can be readily transmitted to another host
}}

CWD prions are transmissible within the Cervidae family. The disease has not been confirmed being transmissible to humans or livestock.<ref>{{cite web |title=CWD: Frequently Asked Questions |url=https://wildlife.tamu.edu/cwdfaq/ |publisher=Texas A&M AgriLife Extension |access-date=24 September 2025}}</ref>

Nevertheless, a 2024 study highlighted a potential link between CWD and human prion disease following the death of two hunters who consumed meat from a CWD-infected deer population. In 2022, a 72-year-old man died within a month of presenting with confusion and aggression after his friend had previously died of Creutzfeldt–Jakob. While the diagnosis was confirmed as sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob, researchers emphasized that cross-species transmission is plausible in animal models and could not be ruled out in this cluster, emphasizing the need for further surveillance.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Trout J, Roberts M, Tabet M, Kotkowski E, Horn S |date=2024-04-09 |title=Two Hunters from the Same Lodge Afflicted with Sporadic CJD: Is Chronic Wasting Disease to Blame? (P7-13.002) |journal=[[Neurology (journal)|Neurology]] |volume=102 |issue=17 Supplement 1 |doi=10.1212/WNL.0000000000204407 |url=https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000204407|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

How the prions that cause CWD spread is unknown, but recent research indicates that prions can be excreted by deer and elk, and are transmitted by eating grass growing in contaminated soil.<ref name=human/> Animals born in captivity and those born in the wild have been affected with the disease. Transmission of CWD is thought to be lateral (from animal to animal). Vertical transmission may occur, although it appears to be relatively unimportant in maintaining epidemics. An infected deer's saliva is able to spread the CWD prions.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Mathiason CK, Powers JG, Dahmes SJ, Osborn DA, Miller KV, Warren RJ, Mason GL, Hays SA, Hayes-Klug J, Seelig DM, Wild MA, Wolfe LL, Spraker TR, Miller MW, Sigurdson CJ, Telling GC, Hoover EA | date = October 6, 2006 | title = Infectious prions in the saliva and blood of deer with chronic wasting disease | journal = Science | volume = 314 | issue = 5796 | pages = 133–6 | pmid = 17023660 | doi = 10.1126/science.1132661| citeseerx = 10.1.1.400.9381 | bibcode = 2006Sci...314..133M | s2cid = 6280366 }}</ref> Exposure between animals is associated with sharing food and water sources contaminated with CWD prions shed by diseased deer.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ernest|first1=Holly B.|last2=Hoar|first2=Bruce R.|last3=Well|first3=Jay A.|last4=O'Rourke|first4=Katherine I.|date=2010-04-01|title=Molecular genealogy tools for white-tailed deer with chronic wasting disease|journal=Canadian Journal of Veterinary Research|volume=74|issue=2|pages=153–156|issn=1928-9022|pmc=2851727|pmid=20592847}}</ref>

==== Direct ====

CWD may be directly transmitted by contact with infected animals, their bodily tissues, and their bodily fluids.<ref name="Saunders-2012">{{Cite journal|title = Occurrence, transmission, and zoonotic potential of chronic wasting disease|last1 = Saunders|first1 = S.E.|date = 2012|journal = Emerging Infectious Diseases|doi = 10.3201/eid1803.110685|last2 = Bartelt-Hunt|first2 = S.L.|issue = 3|volume = 18|pages = 369–376|last3 = Bartz|first3 = J.C.|pmid=22377159|pmc=3309570 }}</ref> Spread may result from contact with infected deer regardless of if they are symptomatic.<ref name="Selariu-2015">{{Cite journal|title = In utero transmission and tissue distribution of chronic wasting disease-associated prions in free-ranging Rocky Mountain elk|last1 = Selariu|first1 = A.|date = 2015|journal = Journal of General Virology|doi = 10.1099/jgv.0.000281|pmid = 26358706|last2 = Powers|first2 = J.G.|last3 = Nalls|first3 = A.|last4 = Brandhuber|first4 = M.|last5 = Mayfield|first5 = A.|last6 = Mathiason|first6 = C.K.|volume=96|issue = 11|pmc=4806583|pages=3444–55}}</ref>

Ticks harbor transmission-relevant quantities of infectious prions; consumption of ticks during grooming (alogrooming), a behavior typical of interactions among female deer and females and young, may contribute to oral prion exposures and between-deer (including maternal to offspring) transmission.<ref name="Inzalaco 2023">{{Cite journal|title = Ticks harbor and excrete chronic wasting disease prions|last1 = Inzalacao|first1 = H.N.|date = 2024|journal = Scientific Reports|last2 = Bravo-Risi|first2 = F.|last3 = Morales|first3 = D.P.|last4 = Walsh|first4 = D.|last5 = Storm|first5 = J.|issue = 13|volume = 1|pages = 7838}}</ref> 

Recent research on Rocky Mountain elk found that with CWD-infected females, many subclinical,  a high rate (80%) of maternal-to-offspring transmission of CWD prions occurred, regardless of gestational period.<ref name="Selariu-2015" /> While not dispositive relative to disease development in the fetus, this does suggest that maternal transmission may be yet another important route of direct CWD transmission.

==== Experimental transmission ====

In addition to the cervid species in which CWD is known to naturally occur, black-tailed deer and European red deer have been demonstrated to be naturally susceptible to CWD.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Chronic wasting disease of captive mule deer: A Spongiform Encepalopathy|last1 = Williams|first1 = E.S.|date = 1980|journal = Journal of Wildlife Diseases|doi = 10.7589/0090-3558-16.1.89|pmid = 7373730|last2 = Young|first2 = S.|volume = 16|issue = 1|pages = 89–98|doi-access = free}}</ref> Other cervid species, including caribou, are also suspected to be naturally vulnerable to this disease.<ref name="Saunders-2012" /> Many other non-cervid mammalian species have been experimentally infected with CWD, either orally or by intracerebral inoculation.<ref name="Saunders-2012" /> These species include monkeys, sheep, cattle, prairie voles, mice, and ferrets.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Could immodulation be used to prevent prion diseases?|last1 = Wisniewski|first1 = T.|date = 2012|journal = Expert Review of Anti-Infective Therapy|doi = 10.1586/eri.11.177|pmid = 22397565|pages = 307–317|volume = 10|issue = 3|last2 = Goni|first2 = F.|pmc = 3321512}}</ref>

An experimental case study of oral transmission of CWD to reindeer shows certain reindeer breeds may be susceptible to CWD, while other subpopulations may be protective against CWD in free-ranging populations. None of the reindeer in the study showed symptoms of CWD, potentially signifying resistance to different CWD strains.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mitchell|first1=Gordon B.|last2=Sigurdson|first2=Christina J.|last3=O'Rourke|first3=Katherine I.|last4=Algire|first4=James|last5=Harrington|first5=Noel P.|last6=Walther|first6=Ines|last7=Spraker|first7=Terry R.|last8=Balachandran|first8=Aru|date=2012-06-18|title=Experimental Oral Transmission of Chronic Wasting Disease to Reindeer (Rangifer tarandus tarandus)|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=7|issue=6|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0039055|issn=1932-6203|pmc=3377593|pmid=22723928|article-number=e39055|bibcode=2012PLoSO...739055M|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Experimental research has also shown that CWD can be transmitted to raccoons via intracerebral inoculation, although with limited efficiency and long incubation periods, suggesting that some non-cervid wildlife may serve as incidental hosts under specific conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Race |first1=Brent |last2=Meade-White |first2=Kimberly D. |last3=Miller |first3=Michael W. |last4=Barbian |first4=Kent D. |last5=Rubenstein |first5=Richard |last6=LaFauci |first6=Giuseppe |last7=Cervenakova |first7=Larisa |last8=Favara |first8=Cynthia |last9=Gardner |first9=Donald |last10=Long |first10=Dan |last11=Parnell |first11=Michael |last12=Striebel |first12=James |last13=Priola |first13=Suzette A. |last14=Ward |first14=Anne |last15=Williams |first15=Elizabeth S. |date=September 2009 |title=Susceptibilities of Nonhuman Primates to Chronic Wasting Disease |url=https://doi.org/10.3201/eid1509.090253 |journal=[[Emerging Infectious Diseases]] |volume=15 |issue=9 |pages=1366–1376 |doi=10.3201/eid1509.090253 |pmid=19788803 |issn=1080-6040 |pmc=2819871}}</ref>

==== Indirect ====

Environmental transmission has been linked to contact with infected bodily fluids and tissues, as well as contact with contaminated environments. Once in the environment, CWD prions may remain infectious for many years<!-- {{vague|date=December 2018}} -->. Thus, decomposition of diseased carcasses, infected "gut piles" from hunters who field dress their cervid harvests, and the urine, saliva, feces, and antler velvet of infected individuals that are deposited in the environment, all have the potential to create infectious environmental reservoirs of CWD.<ref name=2015rev/>

In 2013, researchers at the [[Colorado State University|National Wildlife Research Center]] in [[Fort Collins, Colorado]], successfully infected white-tailed deer with the misfolded prion via the nasal passage, when the prions were mixed with clay.<ref name=nasal>{{cite journal |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0062455|pmid=23671598|pmc=3650006|title=Intranasal Inoculation of White-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus) with Lyophilized Chronic Wasting Disease Prion Particulate Complexed to Montmorillonite Clay|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=8|issue=5|article-number=e62455|year=2013|last1=Nichols|first1=Tracy A.|last2=Spraker|first2=Terry R.|last3=Rigg|first3=Tara D.|last4=Meyerett-Reid|first4=Crystal|last5=Hoover|first5=Clare|last6=Michel|first6=Brady|last7=Bian|first7=Jifeng|last8=Hoover|first8=Edward|last9=Gidlewski|first9=Thomas|last10=Balachandran|first10=Aru|last11=O'Rourke|first11=Katherine|last12=Telling|first12=Glenn C.|last13=Bowen|first13=Richard|last14=Zabel|first14=Mark D.|last15=Vercauteren|first15=Kurt C.|bibcode=2013PLoSO...862455N|doi-access=free}}</ref> This was important because the prions had already been shown by 2006 to bind with sandy quartz clay minerals.<ref name=USDA/>

One avian scavenger, the [[American crow]], was recently evaluated as a potential vector for CWD.<ref name="Fischer-2013">{{Cite journal|title = Could avian scavengers translocated infectious prions to disease-free areas initiating new foci of chronic wasting disease?|last1 = Fischer|first1 = J.W.|date = 2013|journal = Prion|doi = 10.4161/pri.25621|pmid = 23822910|last2 = Phillips|first2 = G.E.|issue = 4|volume = 7|pages = 263–266|last3 = Nichols|first3 = T.A.|last4 = Vercauteren|first4 = K.C.|pmc = 3904308}}</ref> As CWD prions remain viable after passing through the bird's digestive tract, crows represent a possible mechanism for the creation of environmental reservoirs of CWD.<ref name="Fischer-2013" /><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Prion remains infectious after passage through digestive system of American crows (Corvus brachyrhynchos)|last1 = Vercauteren|first1 = K.C.|date = 2012|journal = PLOS ONE|doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0045774|pmid = 23082115|last2 = Pilon|first2 = J.L.|issue = 10|volume = 7|article-number = e45774|last3 = Nash|first3 = P.B.|last4 = Phillips|first4 = G.E.|last5 = Fischer|first5 = J.W.|pmc=3474818|bibcode = 2012PLoSO...745774V|doi-access = free}}</ref> Additionally, the crows' extensive geographic range presents ample opportunities for them to come in contact with CWD.  This, with the added population density and longevity of communal roosting sites in both urban and rural locations, suggests that the fecal deposits at roosting sites may represent a CWD environmental reservoir.<ref name="Fischer-2013" /> Conservative estimates for crows' fecal deposits at one winter roosting site for one winter season ranged from 391,552 to 599,032 kg.<ref name="Fischer-2013" />

CWD prions bind so tightly to soil surface particles that the ground becomes a source of infection and may be a major route of transmission due to frequent ground contact when animals in the deer family graze.<ref name=2015rev/>

==Prevention==
{{Missing information|section|predation|date=December 2020}}
[[File:LDWF CWD Testing Container Site 03.jpg|thumb|[[Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries]] Chronic Wasting Disease Testing Container Site in [[Tallulah, Louisiana]].]]
By 2012, a voluntary system of control was published by [[APHIS]] in the US [[Federal Register]]. It depended on voluntary minimum standards methodology, and herd certification programs to avoid interstate movement of the disease vector. It was based on a [[risk management]] framework.<ref name=USDA/> As of August 2019, APHIS law in 9 CFR Part 55 - CONTROL OF CHRONIC WASTING DISEASE dealt with this problem.

Introduced for the 2019 Minnesota hunting season, a no-cost deer carcass-incineration program was rolled out by Crow Wing County officials hoping to stem the spread of CWD in the region. CWD was found among wild deer in Crow Wing County for the first time in January 2019. The voluntary program encourages both residents and visiting hunters to bring harvested deer carcasses to the county landfill east of Brainerd, Minnesota for incineration and disposal.<ref name="WCTCWDA"/>

In Pennsylvania, the Game Commission established a network of CWD disposal dumpsters across affected regions to help hunters properly dispose of high-risk deer parts such as heads and spinal columns. This initiative, which began in 2018, aims to reduce environmental contamination and prevent the unintentional spread of infectious prions to new areas. Educational outreach and mandatory testing zones were also implemented to increase hunter compliance and awareness.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Game Commission |url=https://www.pa.gov/agencies/pgc.html |access-date=2025-05-06 |website=www.pa.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In 2023, Minnesota funded a [[Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy]] project to assemble 70 public health experts from around the world to devise a response plan for potential human spillover. [[Michael Osterholm]], an infectious disease expert at the [[University of Minnesota]], stressed the urgency of preparedness, noting that the prion responsible for CWD is evolving and becoming more capable of infecting humans. Despite these concerns, a 2022 study by the [[National Institutes of Health]] indicated that the likelihood of prions infecting human brain cells remains remote.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ROBBINS |first=JIM |date=2024-06-06 |title=As 'Zombie' Deer Disease Spreads, Scientists Look for Answers |url=https://e360.yale.edu/features/chronic-wasting-disease-deer |access-date=2024-06-08 |website=Yale E360 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Diagnosis ==
Diagnosis is based on ''post mortem'' examination ([[necropsy]]) and testing; examination of the dead body is not definitive, as many animals die early in the course of the disease and conditions found are nonspecific; general signs of poor health and [[aspiration pneumonia]], which may be the actual cause of death, are common. On microscopic examination, lesions of CWD in the central nervous system resemble those of other TSEs. In addition, scientists use [[immunohistochemistry]] to test [[brain]], [[lymph]], and neuroendocrine tissues for the presence of the abnormal prion protein to diagnose CWD; positive immunohistochemical findings in the [[obex]] is considered the gold standard.<ref name=2015rev/>  Conventional CWD diagnostic strategies and seeded amplification methods for amplifying CWD prions ''in vitro'' include: [[immunohistochemistry]], [[western blotting]], enzyme immunoassay, [[protein misfolding cyclic amplification]], and [[real-time quaking-induced conversion]].<ref name="evdiag">{{cite journal |last1=Haley |first1=Nicholas |last2=Richt |first2=Jurgen |title=Evolution of Diagnostic Tests for Chronic Wasting Disease, a Naturally Occurring Prion Disease of Cervids |journal=Pathogens |date=September 2017 |volume=6 |issue=3 |page=35 |doi=10.3390/pathogens6030035 |pmid=28783058 |pmc=5617992 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Available tests at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency as of July 2019 were not sensitive enough to detect the prion in specimens from animals younger than a year old.<ref name="acia"/>  Strategies are being developed to allow for the quantification of prion burden in a tissue, body fluid, or environmental sample.<ref name="evdiag"/>

As of 2015, no commercially feasible diagnostic tests could be used on live animals.<ref name=2015rev/> As early as 2001 an ''antemortem'' test was deemed urgent.<ref name=p2001/> Running a [[bioassay]], taking fluids from animals in the deer family suspected of infection and incubating them in [[transgenic mice]] that express the cervid prion protein, can be used to determine whether the cervid is infected, but ethical issues exist with this, and it is not scalable.<ref name=2015rev/>

A tonsillar biopsy technique has been a reliable method of testing for CWD in live deer,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wolfe|first1=Lisa L.|last2=Conner|first2=Mary M.|last3=Baker|first3=Thomas H.|last4=Dreitz|first4=Victoria J.|last5=Burnham|first5=Kenneth P.|last6=Williams|first6=Elizabeth S.|last7=Hobbs|first7=N. Thompson|last8=Miller|first8=Michael W.|s2cid=16353279|date=2002|title=Evaluation of Antemortem Sampling to Estimate Chronic Wasting Disease Prevalence in Free-Ranging Mule Deer|journal=The Journal of Wildlife Management|volume=66|issue=3|page=564|doi=10.2307/3803124|jstor=3803124}}</ref> but it only seems to be effective on mule deer and white-tailed deer, not elk.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nwhc.usgs.gov/publications/fact_sheets/pdfs/cwd/cwd012803.pdf |title=Chronic Wasting Disease |website=www.nwhc.usgs.gov |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060912154335/http://www.nwhc.usgs.gov/publications/fact_sheets/pdfs/cwd/cwd012803.pdf|archive-date=2006-09-12 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Biopsies of the rectal mucosa have also been effective at detecting CWD in live mule deer, white-tailed deer, and elk, though detection efficacy may be influenced by numerous factors including animal age, genotype, and disease stage.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Geremia|first1=Chris|last2=Hoeting|first2=Jennifer A.|last3=Wolfe|first3=Lisa L.|last4=Galloway|first4=Nathan L.|last5=Antolin|first5=Michael F.|last6=Spraker|first6=Terry R.|last7=Miller|first7=Michael W.|last8=Hobbs|first8=N. Thompson|date=2015|journal=Journal of Wildlife Diseases|volume=51|issue=4|pages=801–810|doi=10.7589/2014-12-284|pmid=26251986|issn=0090-3558|title=Age and Repeated Biopsy Influence Antemortem PrP<sup>CWD</sup> Testing in Mule Deer (Odocoileus Hemionus) in Colorado, USA|s2cid=176550|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thomsen|first1=Bruce V.|last2=Schneider|first2=David A.|last3=O'Rourke|first3=Katherine I.|last4=Gidlewski|first4=Thomas|last5=McLane|first5=James|last6=Allen|first6=Robert W.|last7=McIsaac|first7=Alex A.|last8=Mitchell|first8=Gordon B.|last9=Keane|first9=Delwyn P.|date=September 2012|title=Diagnostic accuracy of rectal mucosa biopsy testing for chronic wasting disease within white-tailed deer ( Odocoileus virginianus ) herds in North America: Effects of age, sex, polymorphism at PRNP codon 96, and disease progression|journal=Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation|volume=24|issue=5|pages=878–887|doi=10.1177/1040638712453582|pmid=22914819|issn=1040-6387|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Spraker|first1=Terry R.|last2=VerCauteren|first2=Kurt C.|last3=Gidlewski|first3=Thomas|last4=Schneider|first4=David A.|last5=Munger|first5=Randy|last6=Balachandran|first6=Aru|last7=O'Rourke|first7=Katherine I.|date=2009|title=Antemortem Detection of PrP CWD in Preclinical, Ranch-Raised Rocky Mountain Elk ( Cevvus Elaphus Nelsoni ) by Biopsy of the Rectal Mucosa|journal=Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation|volume=21|issue=1|pages=15–24|doi=10.1177/104063870902100103|pmid=19139496|issn=1040-6387|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Monello|first1=Ryan J.|last2=Powers|first2=Jenny G.|last3=Hobbs|first3=N. Thompson|last4=Spraker|first4=Terry R.|last5=O'Rourke|first5=Katherine I.|last6=Wild|first6=Margaret A.|date=April 2013|journal=Journal of Wildlife Diseases|volume=49|issue=2|pages=270–278|doi=10.7589/2011-12-362|pmid=23568902|issn=0090-3558|title=Efficacy of Antemortem Rectal Biopsies to Diagnose and Estimate Prevalence of Chronic Wasting Disease in Free-Ranging Cow Elk (Cervus Elaphus Nelsoni)|s2cid=7698638|doi-access=free}}</ref>

It is possible for CWD prions to [[Autoclave#In medicine|survive sterilization procedures]] involving an autoclave.

== Epidemiology ==
[[File:Distribution of Chronic Wasting Disease in North America. April 2025.jpg|upright=1.6|thumb|Reported cases of chronic wasting disease in North America, as of 2025]]

===North America===
The disease was first identified in 1967 in a closed herd of captive [[mule deer]] in contiguous portions of northeastern Colorado.  In 1980, the disease was determined to be a TSE. It was first identified in wild [[elk]] and mule deer and [[white-tailed deer]] in the early 1980s in Colorado and Wyoming, and in farmed elk in 1997.<ref name=USDA/><ref name=2015rev/><ref name=NWHCFAQ/> The disease did not affect Canada until 1996.<ref name=acia/>

In May 2001, CWD was also found in free-ranging deer in the southwestern corner of [[Nebraska]] (adjacent to Colorado and Wyoming) and later in additional areas in western Nebraska.  The limited area of northern Colorado, southern Wyoming, and western Nebraska in which free-ranging deer, moose, and/or elk positive for CWD have been found is referred to as the [[endemic (epidemiology)|endemic]] area.  The area in 2006 has expanded to six states, including parts of eastern [[Utah]], southwestern [[South Dakota]], and northwestern [[Kansas]].  Also, areas not contiguous (to the endemic area) areas in central Utah and central Nebraska have been found. The limits of the affected areas are not well defined, since the disease is at a low incidence and the amount of sampling may not be adequate to detect it.  In 2002, CWD was detected in wild deer in south-central [[Wisconsin]] and northern [[Illinois]] and in an isolated area of southern [[New Mexico]]. In 2005, it was found in wild [[white-tailed deer]] in [[New York (state)|New York]] and in [[Hampshire County, West Virginia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=WILDLIFE DISEASE |publisher=[[West Virginia Division of Natural Resources]] |date=2008-08-01 |url=http://www.wvdnr.gov/hunting/ChronicWaste.shtm |access-date=2024-04-25}}</ref> In 2008, the first confirmed case of CWD in [[Michigan]] was discovered in an infected deer on an enclosed deer-breeding facility.  It is also found in the Canadian provinces of [[Alberta]] and [[Saskatchewan]].

In February 2011, the [[Maryland]] Department of Natural Resources reported the first confirmed case of the disease in that state. The affected animal was a white-tailed deer killed by a hunter.<ref>{{cite web | date = February 13, 2011 | url = http://www.hometownannapolis.com/news/out/2011/02/13-05/Outdoors-Wasting-disease-confirmed-in-state.html?ne= | title = Wasting Disease Confirmed in State |website=www.hometownannapolis.com}}</ref>

CWD has also been diagnosed in farmed elk and deer herds in a number of states and in two Canadian provinces. The first positive farmed-elk herd in the United States was detected in 1997 in South Dakota.
Since then, additional positive elk herds and farmed white-tailed deer herds have been found in South Dakota (7), Nebraska (4), Colorado (10), [[Oklahoma]] (1), Kansas (1), [[Minnesota]] (3), [[Montana]] (1), Wisconsin (6), and New York (2). As of fall of 2006, four positive elk herds in Colorado and a positive white-tailed deer herd in Wisconsin remain under state [[quarantine]]. All of the other herds have been depopulated or have been slaughtered and tested, and the quarantine has been lifted from one herd that underwent rigorous surveillance with no further evidence of disease. CWD also has been found in farmed elk in the Canadian provinces of [[Saskatchewan]] and [[Alberta]]. A retrospective study also showed mule deer exported from [[Denver]] to the [[Toronto Zoo]] in the 1980s were affected. In June 2015, the disease was detected in a male white-tailed deer on a breeding ranch in [[Medina County, Texas]]. State officials euthanized 34 deer in an effort to contain a possible outbreak.

In February 2018, the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks announced that a [[Mississippi]] deer tested positive for chronic wasting disease.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.clarionledger.com/story/sports/outdoors/2018/02/10/chronic-wasting-disease-deer-mississippi/326042002/ |title=The Clarion Ledger |publisher=The Clarion Ledger |date=2018-02-10 |access-date=2019-02-12}}</ref> Another Mississippi whitetail euthanized in [[Pontotoc County, Mississippi|Pontotoc County]] on 8 October 2018 tested positive for CWD.  The disease was confirmed by the [[National Veterinary Services Laboratory]] in [[Ames, Iowa]] on 30 October 2018.<ref>Times Daily Florence, AL 11/12/18</ref>

Species that have been affected with CWD include elk, mule deer, white-tailed deer, [[black-tailed deer]], and moose. Other [[ruminant]] species, including wild ruminants and domestic [[cattle]], [[sheep]], and [[goat]]s, have been housed in wildlife facilities in direct or indirect contact with CWD-affected deer and elk, with no evidence of disease transmission.  However, experimental transmission of CWD into other ruminants by intracranial inoculation does result in disease, suggesting only a weak molecular species barrier exists. Research is ongoing to further explore the possibility of transmission of CWD to other species.

By April 2016, CWD had been found in captive animals in South Korea; the disease arrived there with live elk that were imported from Canada for farming in the late 1990s.<ref name=USDA/><ref name=NN1stNorway>{{cite news |author=Rachel Becker |website=Nature News |date=April 18, 2016 |url=http://www.nature.com/news/deadly-animal-prion-disease-appears-in-europe-1.19759 |title=Deadly animal prion disease appears in Europe |access-date=2024-04-25}}</ref>

In the summer of 2018, cases were discovered in the Harpur Farm herd in [[Grenville-sur-la-Rouge]], [[Quebec]].<ref name=pourquoi>{{cite news |url=http://www.lapresse.ca/environnement/201810/04/01-5199018-pourquoi-avoir-abattu-3000-cerfs-dans-les-laurentides.php |title=Pourquoi avoir abattu 3000 cerfs dans les Laurentides? | Simon-Olivier Lorange | Environnement |publisher=Lapresse.ca |access-date=2019-02-12|newspaper=La Presse |last1=Lorange |first1=Simon-Olivier }}</ref>

Over the course of 2018, 12% of the [[mule deer]] that were tested in [[Alberta]], had a positive result. More than 8% of Alberta deer were deemed [[seropositive]].<ref name="alberta">{{cite news |title=Critics warn of 'totally unacceptable' risk to humans after meat from 21 tainted elk herds enters food supply |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/elk-contaminated-chronic-wasting-disease-cwd-1.5247570 |publisher=CBC |date=15 August 2019 |access-date=2023-12-27}}</ref>

In 2022, it had been recorded that outbreaks of CWD had shown themselves in both the United States and Canada. CWD was present in 29 states, infecting herds of moose, deer and elk in 391 different counties. Alabama (1), Arkansas (19), Colorado (27), Idaho (1), Illinois (19), Iowa (12), Kansas (49), Louisiana (1), Maryland (1), Michigan (9), Minnesota (7), Mississippi (9), Missouri (21), Montana (23), Nebraska (43), New Mexico (3), New York (1), North Carolina (1), North Dakota (7), Ohio (2), Pennsylvania (14), South Dakota (19), Tennessee (14), Texas (7), Utah (7), Virginia (10), West Virginia (5), Wisconsin (37) and Wyoming (22).

In June 2023, as the spread continued, CWD was found in Oklahoma (1) in the wild <ref>{{Cite web |publisher=National Rifle Association |title=Oklahoma Reports First Case of CWD in Wild Deer |url=https://www.americanhunter.org/content/oklahoma-reports-first-case-of-cwd-in-wild-deer/ |access-date=2023-06-15}}</ref> and Florida (1)<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-15 |title=CWD Confirmed In Florida Deer About 40 Miles From Georgia Line |url=https://gon.com/hunting/cwd-confirmed-in-florida-deer-about-40-miles-from-georgia-line |access-date=2023-06-15 |website=Georgia Outdoor News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Weis |first=Rebecca |date=2023-06-15 |title=Chronic wasting disease detected in Florida |url=https://www.fox4now.com/news/state/chronic-wasting-disease-detected-in-florida |access-date=2024-04-25 |work=Fox 4}}</ref> for the first time. A case in October 2023 in [[Yellowstone National Park]], Wyoming, whose ecosystem supports the greatest and most diverse array of large wild mammals in the continental US, was reported.<ref>{{cite web |last=Wilkinson |first=Todd |title='Zombie deer disease' epidemic spreads in Yellowstone as scientists raise fears it may jump to humans | website=the Guardian | date=22 December 2023 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2023/dec/22/zombie-deer-disease-yellowstone-scientists-fears-fatal-chronic-wasting-disease-cwd-jump-species-barrier-humans-aoe | access-date=22 December 2023}}</ref> The first case in Kentucky was confirmed in December 2023.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://fw.ky.gov/News/Pages/Chronic-wasting-disease-confirmed-in-Kentucky-for-first-time.aspx |title=Chronic Wasting Disease Confirmed in Kentucky for First Time |publisher=Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources |date=December 7, 2023 |access-date=December 8, 2023}}</ref>

In January 2024, British Columbia's surveillance program identified its first two positive deer samples from the Kootenay region of the province.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Forests |first=Ministry of |title=Chronic Wasting Disease - Province of British Columbia |url=https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/plants-animals-ecosystems/wildlife/wildlife-conservation/wildlife-health/chronic-wasting-disease |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=www2.gov.bc.ca}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=February 1, 2024 |title=2 cases of 'zombie deer disease' have been confirmed in B.C. Here's what you need to know |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/chronic-waste-deer-1.7102332 |access-date=2024-04-25 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

In April 2025, the Georgia Department of Natural Resources confirmed a second case of CWD in a 4.5-year-old male deer in Berrien County, approximately 400 yards from the first detected case.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-23 |title=2025 Archives |url=https://cwd-info.org/2025/?utm_s |access-date=2025-05-06 |website=CWD-INFO.ORG |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Quebec farm outbreak ===
[[Quebec]]'s {{interlanguage link|Ministère des Forêts, de la Faune et des Parcs|fr}} practiced 9500 tests in the period between 2007 and autumn 2018 before they detected a seropositive case in September 2018.<ref name=pourquoi/>

The September 2018 discovery of CWD on a managed operation in [[Grenville-sur-la-Rouge]] Quebec prompted a wholesale slaughter of 3500 animals in two months before the enterprise shut down permanently.<ref name="boileau"/> The [[Canadian Food Inspection Agency]] ordered the cull, as well as the decontamination of {{convert|25|cm}} of soil in certain places on the {{convert|400|ha|adj=on}} operation.<ref name=pourquoi/> Post-discovery, each animal was tested for CWD by the Food Inspection Agency before it was released onto the market. Other Quebec producers lamented the glut of supply.<ref name="boileau">{{cite news |title= DU CERF DE BOILEAU, IL N'Y EN AURA PLUS  |url=http://plus.lapresse.ca/screens/6c5513c6-1060-4819-9b93-f8a6f6562acb__7C___0.html |publisher=La Presse, ltée |date=21 December 2018 |access-date=2023-12-27}}</ref> A 400 km<sup>2</sup> quarantine area was declared, in which all hunting and trapping activities were banned.<ref name="qq">{{cite news |title=Une maladie fatale affectant les cerfs arrive au Québec |first=Morgan|last=Lowrie |url=https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/environnement/201809/30/01-5198535-une-maladie-fatale-affectant-les-cerfs-arrive-au-quebec.php |publisher=La Presse Canadienne |date=1 October 2018 |access-date=2023-12-27}}</ref> The government slaughtered hundreds of wild animals over a two-month period. The routine cull for market was between 70 and 100 animals per week. When the producer was forced to close, the weekly slaughter neared 500 animals per week.<ref name=boileau/> One year later, 750 wild specimens had been culled in the 45 km-radius "enhanced monitoring area", and none tested positive for CWD.<ref name=cbcmffp/>
It came to light in August 2019 that prior to 2014 in Canada, all animals on CWD-infected farms were buried or incinerated. Since 2014, however, the Food Inspection Agency has allowed animals from CWD-infected farms to enter the food chain because there is "no national requirement to have animals tested for the disease". From one CWD-infected herd in Alberta, 131 elk were sold for human consumption.<ref name=alberta/>

For the fall 2019 hunting season in western Quebec, the provincial ministry relaxed the rules for the annual white-tailed deer hunt, in an effort to curb the spread of CWD. Any white-tailed deer can be hunted with any weapon in certain municipalities in the [[Outaouais]] valley and the [[Laurentides]]. The Ministère des Forêts hopes thereby to receive more samples to test for CWD.<ref name="cbcmffp">{{cite news |title=Deer hunting rules relaxed to curb deadly disease |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/relaxed-rules-hunting-deer-chronic-wasting-disease-1.5275446 |publisher=CBC |date=9 September 2019 |access-date=2023-12-27}}</ref> The quarantine around Grenville was still in place, and the ministry specifically prohibited (only) the "removal" from the quarantine "enhanced monitoring area" zone of "the head, more specifically any part of the brain, the [[eyes]], the [[Retropharyngeal space|retropharyngeal]] [[lymph nodes]] and the [[tonsils]], any part of the [[spinal column]], the internal organs (including the [[liver]] and the [[heart]]), and the [[testicles]]."<ref name="mffpqa">{{cite web |title=Operation to control and monitor chronic wasting disease in cervids |url=https://mffp.gouv.qc.ca/the-wildlife/chronic-wasting-disease-cervids/?lang=en#coord-mdc |publisher=mffp.gouv.qc.ca |date=29 August 2019 |access-date=9 September 2019 |archive-date=26 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190626013008/https://mffp.gouv.qc.ca/the-wildlife/chronic-wasting-disease-cervids/?lang=en#coord-mdc |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Europe ===
====Nordics====
In 2016, the first case of CWD in Europe was from the Nordfjella wild reindeer herd in southern [[Norway]]. Scientists found the diseased female reindeer as it was dying, and routine CWD screening at necropsy was unexpectedly positive. The origin of CWD in Norway is unknown, whereas import of infected deer from Canada was the source of CWD cases in [[South Korea]]. Norway has strict legislation and rules not allowing importation of live animals and deer into the country. Norway has a [[scrapie]] surveillance program since 1997; while no reports of scrapie within the range of Nordfjella reindeer population have been identified, sheep are herded through that region and are a potential source of infection.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benestad|first1=Sylvie L. |last2=Mitchell|first2=Gordon |last3=Simmons|first3=Marion |last4=Ytrehus|first4=Bjørnar |last5=Vikøren|first5=Turid |date=2016-01-01 |title=First case of chronic wasting disease in Europe in a Norwegian free-ranging reindeer |journal=Veterinary Research |volume=47 |issue=1|page=88 |doi=10.1186/s13567-016-0375-4 |issn=0928-4249 |pmc=5024462 |pmid=27641251 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In May and June 2016, two infected wild moose (''[[Alces alces]]'') were found around {{convert|300|km}} north from the first case, in [[Selbu Municipality]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Chronic Wasting Disease in Norway |url=http://www.mattilsynet.no/language/english/animals/chronic_wasting_disease_in_norway.23274 |website=Norwegian Food Safety Authority |access-date=2018-03-12 |date=15 September 2016 |archive-date=23 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190223184644/https://www.mattilsynet.no/language/english/animals/chronic_wasting_disease_in_norway.23274|url-status=dead}}</ref> By the end of August, a fourth case had been confirmed in a wild reindeer shot in the same area as the first case in March.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nytt tilfelle av CWD på villrein |url=http://www.vetinst.no/nyheter/nytt-tilfelle-cwd-pa-rein |website=Norwegian Veterinary Institute |access-date=2018-03-12 |language=no |date=29 August 2016}}</ref>

In 2017, the [[Norwegian Environment Agency]] released guidelines for hunters hunting reindeer in the Nordfjella areas. The guidelines contain information on identifying animals with CWD symptoms and instructions for minimizing the risk of contamination, as well as a list of supplies given to hunters to be used for taking and submitting samples from shot reindeer.<ref>{{cite web |title=Informasjon til villreinjegere i Nordfjella |trans-title=Information for reindeer hunters in Nordfjella |url=http://www.miljodirektoratet.no/Documents/publikasjoner/M787/M787.pdf |access-date=2018-03-12 |language=no |date=2017 |archive-date=17 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170817204809/http://www.miljodirektoratet.no/Documents/publikasjoner/M787/M787.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In March 2018, Finnish Food Safety Authority EVIRA stated that the first case of CWD in Finland had been diagnosed in a 15-year-old moose (''Alces alces'') that had died naturally in the municipality of [[Kuhmo]] in the [[Kainuu]] region. Before this case in Kuhmo, [[Norway]] was the only country in the [[European Economic Area]] where CWD has been diagnosed. The moose did not have the transmissible North American form of the disease, but similar to the Norwegian variant of CWD, an atypical or sporadic form which occurs incidentally in individual animals of the deer family. In Finland, CWD screening of fallen wild deer has been done since 2003. None of the roughly 2,500 samples analyzed so far have tested positive for the disease. The export of live animals of the deer family to other countries has been temporarily banned as a precautionary measure to stop the spread of the CWD, and moose hunters are going to be provided with more instructions before the start of the next hunting season, if appropriate. The export and sales of meat from deer will not be restricted and moose meat is considered safe to eat as only the brain and nervous tissue of infected moose contains prions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Moose found dead in forest with chronic wasting disease |url=https://www.evira.fi/en/animals/current_issues/2018/moose-found-dead-in-forest-with-chronic-wasting-disease/ |website=Evira |access-date=2018-03-12 |date=8 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624150546/https://www.evira.fi/en/animals/current_issues/2018/moose-found-dead-in-forest-with-chronic-wasting-disease/ |archive-date=24 June 2018 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In March 2019, the [[National Veterinary Institute (Sweden)|Swedish National Veterinary Institute]] diagnosed the first case of CWD in Sweden. A 16-year old emaciated female moose was found in the municipality of [[Arjeplog Municipality|Arjeplog]] in the county of [[Norrbotten County|Norrbotten]], circling and with loss of shyness towards humans, possibly blind. The moose was euthanized and the head was sent for CWD screening in the national CWD surveillance program. The brainstem tissue, but not lymph nodes, was positive for CWD (confirmed with Western Blot). A second case of CWD was diagnosed in May 2019, with very similar case history, about 70 km east of the first case. This second case, in the municipality of [[Arvidsjaur Municipality|Arvidsjaur]], was also an emaciated and apathic 16-year-old female moose that was euthanized. The circumstances of these Swedish cases are similar to the CWD cases in moose in both Norway and Finland. The EU regulated CWD surveillance runs between 2018 – 2020. A minimum of 6,000 deer are to be tested, both free-ranging animals in the deer family, farmed red deer, and semi-domesticated reindeer.<ref name="Aktuellt">{{Cite web |url=https://www.sva.se/aktuellt/nyheter/avmagringssjuka-cwd-upptackt-pa-alg-i-norrbottens-lan/ |title=Avmagringssjuka (CWD) upptäckt på älg i Norrbottens län |trans-title=Wasting disease (CWD) discovered in moose in Norrbotten County |website=www.sva.se |access-date=2024-04-25 |language=sv |date=2019-03-26 |archive-date=25 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240425211506/https://www.sva.se/aktuellt/nyheter/avmagringssjuka-cwd-upptackt-pa-alg-i-norrbottens-lan/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The finding of CWD-positive moose initiated an intensified surveillance in the affected municipalities. Adult hunter-harvested moose and slaughtered semi-domesticated reindeer from the area are tested for CWD. In September 2019, a third moose was found positive for CWD, a hunter-harvested 10-year-old apparently healthy female moose from Arjeplog.<ref name="Aktuellt"/> A fourth case of CWD in moose was verified in September 2020, in a euthanized 14-year-old lame and unshy female moose in the municipality of Robertsfors, in the county of Västerbotten, approximately 200 km from the previous moose cases in the neighboring county of Norrbotten.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.mynewsdesk.com/se/jordbruksverket/pressreleases/nytt-fall-av-avmagringssjuka-cwd-paa-aelg-3037551 |title = Nytt fall av avmagringssjuka (CWD) på älg |trans-title=New case of wasting disease (CWD) in moose (tr.: elk?) |website=www.mynewsdesk.com |date = 24 September 2020 |access-date=2024-04-25 |language=no}}</ref>

==Research==
{{Scholia|topic}}
Research is focused on better ways to monitor disease in the wild, live animal diagnostic tests, developing vaccines, better ways to dispose of animals that died from the disease and to decontaminate the environment, where prions can persist in soils, and better ways to monitor the food supply. Deer harvesting and management issues are intertwined.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.google.com/search?q=www.freep.com%2Fstory%2Fsports%2Foutdoors%2F2017%2F11%2F26%2Fhunters-must-change-approach-help-stall-cwd-spreading-humans |title=Hunters must change approach, help stall CWD from spreading to humans |first1=Lydia |last1=Lohrer |newspaper=[[Detroit Free Press]] |date=November 26, 2017 |access-date=November 26, 2017}}</ref> Additionally, scientists are investigating genetic resistance to CWD in certain deer populations, with the goal of understanding whether selective breeding or natural selection could help slow disease spread. Public outreach and hunter education programs have also become a key part of management strategies, aiming to improve compliance with carcass disposal regulations, testing requirements, and movement restrictions in affected regions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seabury |first1=Christopher M |last2=Oldeschulte |first2=David L |last3=Bhattarai |first3=Eric K |last4=Legare |first4=Dhruti |last5=Ferro |first5=Pamela J |last6=Metz |first6=Richard P |last7=Johnson |first7=Charles D |last8=Lockwood |first8=Mitchell A |last9=Nichols |first9=Tracy A |date=2020-04-01 |title=Accurate Genomic Predictions for Chronic Wasting Disease in U.S. White-Tailed Deer |url=https://doi.org/10.1534/g3.119.401002 |journal= G3 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=1433–1441 |doi=10.1534/g3.119.401002 |pmid=32122960 |issn=2160-1836|pmc=7144088 }}</ref>

extract:
Chronic wasting disease (CWD), sometimes called zombie deer disease, is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy (TSE) naturally affecting members of the deer family. TSEs are a family of diseases caused by misfolded proteins called prions and include similar diseases such as mad cow disease in cattle, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in humans, and scrapie in sheep. In the United States, CWD affects mule deer, white-tailed deer, red deer, sika deer, elk, caribou, and moose. The transmission of CWD to other species such as squirrel monkeys and humanized mice has been observed in experimental settings.
In 1967, CWD was first identified in mule deer at a government research facility in northern Colorado, United States. It was initially recognized as a clinical "wasting" syndrome and then in 1978, it was identified more specifically as a TSE disease. Since then, CWD has been found in free-ranging and captive animal populations in 33 US states and five Canadian provinces. In addition, CWD has been found in one Minnesota red deer farm, one wild reindeer herd in Norway (March 2016) as well as in wild moose. Single cases of CWD in moose have been found in Finland (March 2018) and in Sweden (March and May 2019, September 2020). CWD was found in South Korea in some deer imported from Canada. CWD is typified by chronic weight loss and clinical signs compatible with brain lesions, aggravated over time, always leading to death. 
Although reports in the popular press have been made of humans being affected by CWD, a 2004 study for the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention concluded that "more epidemiologic and laboratory studies are needed to monitor the possibility of such transmissions". A 2019 study added that "the potential exists for transmission to humans and subsequent human disease". The epidemiological study further concluded, "as a precaution, hunters should avoid eating deer and elk tissues known to harbor the CWD agent (e.g., brain, spinal cord, eyes, spleen, tonsils, lymph nodes) from areas where CWD has been identified". In April 2024, it was revealed that two men from the same hunting group contracted Creutzfeldt–Jakob, prompting medical researchers to speculate transmission had occurred from consuming CWD-positive venison.
